content.title: About
content.content: Ladyfinger cookies are light, dry biscuits shaped like thin sticks, resembling delicate fingers. They are made from flour, sugar, eggs, and butter, sometimes flavored with vanilla or lemon zest. The cookies are crisp, mildly sweet, and often used in desserts such as tiramisu.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “ladyfinger” comes from the shape of the biscuit, which looks like elegant fingers.
Ladyfingers are a traditional ingredient in the Italian dessert tiramisu.
In some countries the biscuit is called “savoiardi,” a reference to the Savoy region in France.
The thin sticks allow the cookie to absorb syrups and creams quickly without losing shape.
They are frequently used in layered desserts, such as trifle.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Traditional recipes contain only a modest amount of butter, making them less calorie‑dense than many richer cookies.

items.title: Source of quick carbs
items.content: Sugar and flour provide a rapid source of energy, useful for a light snack.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs add a small amount of plant‑based protein to the biscuit.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: Ladyfingers pair easily with fruit, yogurt, or cottage cheese, enhancing the nutritional profile of a snack.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Unlike many savory crackers, ladyfingers typically contain little to no added salt.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The biscuits contain wheat flour and are not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: High sugar levels may be unsuitable for individuals with diabetes or those monitoring sugar intake.

items.title: Cavity risk
items.content: Sweet biscuits can contribute to tooth decay if consumed frequently without proper oral hygiene.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some commercial versions may contain preservatives or artificial flavors that could trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ladyfingers can be enjoyed as a light snack on their own, used in desserts (tiramisu, trifle), dipped in coffee or tea, or paired with fruit sauces, yogurt, or ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and maintain crispness.

shrimp-and-vegetables-excluding-carrots-.title: Shrimp and vegetables (no carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens, potatoes, sauce)

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp are a low‑calorie seafood with a delicate flavor and high nutritional value. Combined with a variety of vegetables such as bell pepper, zucchini and tomatoes, they create a light dish that excludes carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens, potatoes and sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp belong to the crustacean family and are among the most widely consumed seafood worldwide.
They can change the color of their exoskeleton depending on the environment.
Shrimp are rich in astaxanthin, a powerful antioxidant not found in many other foods.
The vegetables used are often grown without pesticides, enhancing their nutritional profile.
A sauce‑free preparation preserves the natural taste of the ingredients and makes it easier to control sodium intake.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Shrimp provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Less than 1 g of fat per 100 g makes shrimp suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium supports immune function and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Shrimp are rich in vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Vegetable‑derived fiber and vitamins
items.content: Bell pepper, zucchini and tomatoes supply vitamin C, vitamin A and dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Choose shrimp from reputable sources to avoid mercury or cadmium exposure.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can lead to bacterial growth and food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté shrimp on high heat for 2‑3 minutes until pink. Cut vegetables into bite‑size pieces and lightly steam or roast them until tender. Combine in one pan, finish with a splash of lemon juice and fresh herbs for aroma. Serve as a standalone meal or alongside whole‑grain rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh shrimp in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C and use within 2 days. Store vegetables in the crisper drawer in a sealed bag. For longer keeping, freeze shrimp in an airtight container for up to 3 months; freeze vegetables separately to maintain texture.
